site.title: English 135
colophon: A way through the course W. H. Auden gave at the University of Michigan in the fall of 1941. The [Sources](#/about) page says what is documented and what the site itself supplies.
The books printed here are in the public domain in the United States. What you write is kept in this browser and nowhere else.

book.title: Your book
book.intro: In 1970 Auden published *A Certain World*, which he called a commonplace book: passages from his reading, set under headings, with his comments. This page is yours. It holds the lines you kept while reading, the words you put into the gaps beside the writers’ own, your answers beside Auden’s, your verdicts, and what you made.

heart.kicker: One of Auden’s ways into a poem
heart.title: By heart
heart.intro: Auden asked the Michigan class to learn cantos of Dante by heart. One student, Angelyn Stevens, pinned typed pages of the poem over her kitchen sink and learned them while she did the dishes. In 1978 Robert Chapman, who took the course, reported that some of his classmates said they still had eight cantos by heart.

No place has been found where he sets out his reasons at length. In the college for poets he daydreams about in *The Dyer’s Hand*, the students learn thousands of lines by heart. In an interview for the *Paris Review* near the end of his life he was asked whether he had ever taught writing. He said he had not, and that if he had to teach poetry he would keep to prosody, rhetoric, philology and getting poems by heart.
Learn a few lines and write them out from memory, and the page shows you each place where your memory put in a word of its own. It is the missing-word sheet again, with every word missing.
heart.cantos.title: What Auden asked of the class
heart.cantos.intro: The final examination of the course was the cantos, written out from memory in three hours. Most accounts say six cantos. Donald Pearce, who took the examination, says seven, brought down to five when the class protested. This site follows Pearce, keeps the four cantos he names and leaves the fifth to you.
They are here if you want them, and the examination can be taken whenever you like.

heart.set.title: Nine lines to begin with
heart.set.intro: The words over the gate of Hell are the first thing Dante reads when he gets there.
heart.how.title: A way of learning lines
heart.how: Read the lines aloud until you can hear where they go.
Under Learn, a piece comes a few lines at a time. Write each stretch with the text open, then with only the first letter of each word showing, then with the text covered.
Under Write out, write the whole from memory and compare it with the text. The page shows you every word your memory changed.
If someone will listen, say it aloud to them.
heart.rule: The site calls a piece known when you have written it out on two different days with no more than one word in a hundred wrong, left out or put in. Spelling matters, except that the British and American spellings of a word, such as *colour* and *color*, are taken as the same. Capitals, punctuation, accents and line breaks are ignored.
This rule is the site’s. Little is recorded of how Auden graded the examination, and the [Sources](#/about) page gives what there is.

cantos.title: The cantos
cantos.intro: Donald Pearce, a student in the class, says that Auden first asked for seven cantos and came down to five when the class protested. Pearce names four of the seven: *Inferno* III and V, *Purgatorio* XXVIII and *Paradiso* XXXIII. This site keeps those four and leaves the fifth to you.

final.title: Five cantos from memory
final.intro: Four or five weeks before the final, Auden told the class that it would be a written examination of three hours, held after the Christmas vacation. They would write out from memory seven cantos of the *Divine Comedy* in the prose translation of Carlyle, Okey and Wicksteed. The class called it impossible, and he cut the seven to five. Before he drove to California for Christmas he promised to telephone and cancel the examination if he could not learn the five himself by the time he reached Los Angeles. He did not telephone, and the examination was held.
Donald Pearce, the student who tells this, wrote for the three hours and filled five blue books.
final.paper.title: The five cantos
final.rules.title: Rules
final.rules: You have three hours from the moment you begin, and the clock does not stop.
There is a box for each canto, in the order of the poem. Fill them in any order. Nothing can be pasted in.
When the time is up, or when you hand in, what you have written is compared with the text word by word.

A canto passes if no more than one word in a hundred is wrong, left out or put in. Spelling counts, but the British and American spellings of a word are taken as the same. Capitals, punctuation, accents and line breaks do not count.
You pass the examination when all five cantos pass. You may take it again, and every attempt is recorded.

notebook.keep.title: Keeping your work
notebook.keep: Your book is stored in this browser on this device. If the browser’s data is cleared, the book goes with it, so save a copy now and then.

“Save a copy” downloads one file that holds everything you have done here, and the file can be restored later. “Download as plain text” gives a second file, which is for reading and printing only. To move to another device, carry the saved copy there, open this page and choose “Restore from a copy.” Restoring replaces everything now in that browser with what is in the copy.
